description: 🚀 Horizon Heroes is an ambitious high school team aiming to make lunar exploration safer and smarter! For the 2026NASA SpaceAppsChallenge, we’re developing the Lunar Landing Site Navigator—an interactive tool designed to analyze and visualize optimal Moon landing spots using NASA's open-source lunar datasets (like LRO/LOLA). We're in our starting phase and would love to collaborate! Looking for team members interested in coding, data analysis/visualization, UI design, or creative storytelling.
summary:
"Lunar Landing Site Navigator" is an interactive 3D digital mapping tool developed by "Horizon Heroes" to simplify, evaluate, and navigate optimal touchdown spots on the Moon for future robotic and crewed missions.

Safe lunar landing requires identifying flat terrains, dodging hazards, and securing resources like water ice and sunlight. Our solution utilizes open-source data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)—including LOLA (elevation) and Diviner (temperature)—and translates complex planetary files into an intuitive, accessible web-based navigator.

The application evaluates candidate sites based on user-weighted parameters like slope safety, illumination, and communication lines. Users can inspect terrains, measure hazard levels, and plan initial rover traversal routes in 3D.

As high school innovators, we designed this project to bridge raw space agency data with collaborative decision-making, helping explorers navigate the challenging lunar South Pole. It lowers the barrier to mission planning and invites everyone to help lay the foundation for humanity's multi-planetary future.
details:
What does it do & How does it work? The Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web-based geographic information system (GIS) custom-built for moon explorations. It allows users to browse potential landing sites, choose parameters (such as 'Maximum Allowable Slope' or 'Required Sunlight Exposure'), and generates a heat-mapped safety overlay on top of a 3D Moon interface. The user selects a ROI (Region of Interest), and the navigator highlights the safest zones and identifies possible resource hotspots like water ice inside PSRs (Permanently Shadowed Regions).

Tools, Coding Languages & Data Used:

  • Languages: Python for back-end data processing and API integration; HTML5/JavaScript (using libraries like Three.js, CesiumJS, or Leaflet) for the 3D map renderer and interactive UI.
  • Databases & Datasets: We primarily sourced data from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) mission. Specifically, we used LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) DEMs for topography and slope calculations, and Diviner data for thermal and ice-retention analysis.
  • Development Tools: VS Code, QGIS for testing dataset overlays, GitHub for collaboration, and Figma for prototyping the UI.

How is it creative & What factors did we consider? While professional aerospace tools are heavily gatekept and complex, our "Navigator" gamifies and simplifies the landing search. Its novelty lies in a real-time weight-customization slider, letting users dynamically change mission constraints (e.g., "high-sunlight/low-weight" robot landers vs. "flat terrain/safe-crater" habitation).

We prioritized natural UX/UI, 3D lunar terrain mesh rendering (allowing realistic shadow forecasting based on solar position), and high accuracy—basing every pixel on genuine, scaled NASA topographic elevation. Ultimately, we wanted a platform where anyone—from students to mission teams—can inspect and interact with the South Pole landscapes in seconds.
